issues.legal_issue: A short delay in filing an appeal should be condoned when a justice-oriented assessment establishes sufficient cause and refusing condonation would prevent a potentially meritorious matter from being decided on its merits.
material_facts: The appeal challenged an enhancement of compensation for acquired land that raised important questions about valuation.
The appeal was filed four days beyond the prescribed period.
The Court was satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay and that the appeal should be considered on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The delay was condoned, the order dismissing the appeal as time-barred was set aside, and the matter was remitted for decision on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a late appeal to be admitted where sufficient cause is shown. The phrase “sufficient cause” is elastic and should be applied rationally and pragmatically to advance substantial justice. Courts should not presume that delay was deliberate, caused by culpable negligence, or mala fide; a demand to explain every day is not a call for a pedantic approach. Where substantial justice conflicts with technical considerations, a non-deliberate delay should not ordinarily defeat a merits decision. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: appeal_dismissed_as_time_barred and short_delay and important_merits_questions and sufficient_cause_for_delay

predicates.appeal_dismissed_as_time_barred: An appeal was rejected because it was filed after the prescribed period.
predicates.short_delay: The appeal was filed only a short time after the prescribed period expired.
predicates.important_merits_questions: The appeal raised important questions that warranted determination on their merits.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay: The circumstances of the delay were found to provide sufficient cause for filing late.

issues.definition: When an appeal is time-barred by a short delay, raises important merits questions, and the circumstances provide sufficient cause, the delay is condoned.

issues.legal_issue: A government litigant seeking condonation of delay is entitled to the same equitable application of the sufficient-cause standard as any other litigant.
material_facts: The application for condonation was made by the State in an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
The High Court rejected the application and dismissed the appeal as time-barred.
The Supreme Court held that the State's identity as the applicant was irrelevant to the standard to be applied and that it was entitled to even-handed treatment.
issues.conclusion: The State was not to be treated more harshly or more leniently than other litigants; the same equitable standard applied to its application for condonation.
issues.legal_principle: The principle of equality before law requires courts to treat all litigants, including the State, even-handedly when applying Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The State does not have a special disfavoured status, and its status as a government litigant does not itself determine whether sufficient cause exists. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.delay_condonation_proceeding: A litigant asks a court to excuse a delay in filing an appeal or application.
predicates.applicant_is_state: The litigant seeking to excuse the delay is the State.

issues.definition: When the State seeks to excuse delay, it receives the same limitation standard as other litigants.
